clues: Possesses both receptor affinity and positive intrinsic activity.
Stabilizes the active conformation of a receptor to trigger intracellular signaling.
A ligand that binds to a receptor and activates it to produce a biological response.
Shifts an agonist's log dose-response curve parallel to the right without lowering Emax.
Its blockade can be overcome by increasing the concentration of the agonist.
A drug that binds reversibly to the same receptor site as an agonist with zero intrinsic activity.
Buprenorphine and pindolol are well-known clinical examples.
Has an intrinsic activity strictly between 0 and 1.
Binds to a receptor to produce a submaximal effect and can antagonize a full agonist.
Requires a receptor system that exhibits constitutive basal activity.
Beta-carbolines acting at GABA-A receptors are a classic example.
A ligand that stabilizes the inactive receptor state and lowers basal activity below baseline.
Determined by the drug's affinity for its receptor and receptor reserve.
Measured by the EC50 or ED50 on a graded dose-response curve.
The amount or concentration of a drug required to produce an effect of a given magnitude.
Represented by the plateau (Emax) on a graded dose-response curve.
Distinguishes a full agonist from a partial agonist regardless of dose.
The maximum biological response that a drug can elicit upon binding its receptor.
Drugs like digoxin, lithium, and warfarin have a very narrow value for this parameter.
Calculated as TD50 (or LD50) divided by ED50.
A quantitative ratio comparing the toxic dose of a drug to its effective dose as a measure of safety.
Occur when EC50 is substantially lower than the receptor dissociation constant Kd.
Explain why low doses of an irreversible antagonist initially shift the dose-response curve right before lowering Emax.
Receptor reserve in which a full maximal tissue response is achieved without occupying all available receptors.
Classically seen with repeated closely spaced doses of ephedrine or continuous nitroglycerin.
Occurs within minutes to hours rather than weeks.
Acute, rapid loss of responsiveness to a drug following repeated administration.
Explains why abrupt withdrawal of propranolol can trigger rebound angina or hypertension.
Triggered by prolonged receptor blockade or chronic denervation.
An increase in the number of functional cell-surface receptors leading to supersensitivity.
Possesses seven transmembrane alpha-helical domains.
Includes beta-adrenoceptors, muscarinic receptors, and opioid receptors.
A metabotropic cell-surface receptor that signals through heterotrimeric GTP-binding proteins.
Activated by Gq-coupled receptors such as alpha-1 adrenergic and M3 muscarinic receptors.
Cleaves membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
The effector enzyme that generates the two second messengers IP3 and diacylglycerol.
Produces cellular responses within milliseconds.
Nicotinic acetylcholine and GABA-A receptors belong to this family.
An ionotropic receptor that directly opens a transmembrane pore for ions upon neurotransmitter binding.
Allopurinol and clavulanic acid act by this mechanism.
Also known as mechanism-based enzyme inactivation.
A substrate analogue converted by the target enzyme itself into a reactive product that covalently inactivates it.
Benzodiazepines act in this manner at the GABA-A receptor.
Does not compete directly with the endogenous ligand for the primary binding pocket.
A substance that binds to a distinct regulatory site on a receptor to enhance or reduce agonist activity.
